title: ITA Section 127(18)-(20): SR&ED Government Assistance
keyPhrase: ITA Section 127(18) to (20) SR&ED government assistance
description: Understand how grants and subsidies impact your Canadian R&D claim under ITA Section 127(18) to (20) legislation on SR&ED government assistance reductions.
summary: Under the federal Income Tax Act's government assistance reduction rules, Canadian SR&ED claimants must reduce their qualified SR&ED expenditures and section 37 deduction pool by any government assistance, non-government assistance or provincial R&D tax credit received, receivable or reasonably expected, reported on Line 513 of Form T661. Repayments of that assistance are added back, preventing double subsidization of expenditures.

body.text: Under the federal Income Tax Act's government assistance reduction rules, Canadian SR&ED claimants must reduce their qualified SR&ED expenditures and section 37 deduction pool by any government assistance, non-government assistance or provincial R&D tax credit received, receivable or reasonably expected, reported on Line 513 of Form T661. Repayments of that assistance are added back, preventing double subsidization of expenditures.
Executive Overview and Macro-Fiscal Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives

Canada operates one of the most mature and financially significant research and development tax incentive regimes in the industrialized world, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. The federal government has provided statutory tax assistance for industrial research and development since 1944, establishing the modern structural framework of the SR&ED program in 1994 under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA). As the single largest federal program supporting business R&D in Canada, the SR&ED regime delivers multi-billion-dollar annual support across all sectors of the Canadian economy, with approximately 26,000 businesses and individual claimants receiving $2.8 billion in direct tax assistance through the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) in a single benchmark reporting cycle. Several provincial and territorial jurisdictions reinforce this federal foundation with parallel corporate tax credits that generally mirror the federal definition of eligible work while applying distinct regional credit rates, expenditure caps, and refundability parameters.

Despite its scale, the macro-fiscal trajectory of the Canadian R&D landscape experienced a prolonged structural contraction between the early 2000s and the late 2010s that ultimately catalyzed comprehensive legislative reform between 2024 and 2026. Total SR&ED expenditures claimed by businesses in Canada declined by 30% from a historical peak of nearly $19.6 billion in 2001 to $13.6 billion in 2016. Similarly, after reaching a zenith of approximately 27,500 participating firms in 2009, the number of enterprises claiming SR&ED tax credits contracted consecutively for several years, falling by 23% between 2009 and 2016. This multi-year erosion reflected earlier legislative restrictions—most notably the elimination of capital expenditures and capital lease costs from SR&ED eligibility after December 31, 2013, alongside the reduction of the basic corporate ITC rate to 15%—which diminished the effective after-tax subsidy for capital-intensive manufacturing, clean technology, and scaling mid-market corporations.

Recognizing that declining business enterprise R&D intensity threatened domestic productivity and intellectual property retention, the Department of Finance Canada initiated a comprehensive two-phase national consultation on the SR&ED program in early 2024. The first phase of public consultations ran from January 31, 2024, to April 15, 2024, culminating in policy commitments alongside Budget 2024: Fairness for Every Generation, while the second phase of consultations extended until May 27, 2024. These consultations examined how the SR&ED program could better support the growth of R&D-intensive Canadian businesses, what structural improvements to the statutory definition of SR&ED and its eligibility criteria were warranted, how the program could complement direct grant ecosystems, and how tax policy could ensure the domestic retention of intellectual property so that innovative firms remain Canadian-owned and operated. Following the Department of Finance's December 2024 reform announcement and the release of detailed draft legislative amendments to the Income Tax Act in August 2025, Parliament enacted sweeping statutory enhancements to the SR&ED program through the Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, with retroactive operational effect for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, and depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024.

These 2024–2026 legislative reforms represent the most consequential modernization of Canadian R&D tax law in over three decades. The enacted framework doubles the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million, expands the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the legacy $10 million–$50 million corridor to a substantially broader $15 million–$75 million corridor, extends access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time, and restores the eligibility of capital expenditures and shared-use equipment (SUE) for both section 37 income deductions and section 127 investment tax credits. Concurrently, major provincial jurisdictions have enacted parallel structural alignments—most notably Ontario's harmonization with the federal restoration of capital expenditures effective December 16, 2024, and Québec's March 25, 2025 budgetary consolidation of six legacy R&D tax credits into the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC).
Statutory and Legislative Framework Under the Federal Income Tax Act

Unlike jurisdictions that rely upon a notional "super-deduction" mechanism (whereby corporate taxpayers deduct an inflated multiple exceeding 100% of actual R&D outlays against taxable income), Canada's federal tax architecture bifurcates R&D relief into two distinct, cumulative statutory mechanisms under the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)): an immediate 100% income deduction pool under section 37, and a direct Investment Tax Credit (ITC) applied against Part I tax payable or refunded in cash under sections 127 and 127.1.
The Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1)

The legal gateway to both federal and provincial R&D tax relief in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statutory architecture divides qualifying scientific and technological activities into three foundational categories—basic research, applied research, and experimental development—supplemented by a fourth category of directly attributable support work and bounded by seven explicit statutory exclusions.

Basic research, governed by paragraph 248(1)(a), encompasses systematic work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Applied research, governed by paragraph 248(1)(b), similarly comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge, but is conducted with a specific practical application in view. Experimental development, governed by paragraph 248(1)(c) and representing the overwhelming majority of industrial claims in Canada, consists of systematic work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Under paragraph 248(1)(d), ancillary technical activities with respect to engineering, design (defined by the Canada Revenue Agency as work to transform concepts and ideas into a plan), operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research also qualify as SR&ED, but strictly to the extent that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Conversely, the work identified in paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) is collectively designated in CRA policy as "excluded work" or "the exclusions". This statutorily excluded work—which never qualifies as SR&ED—encompasses market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.
Immediate Deductibility and Expenditure Pooling: Section 37

Section 37 of the ITA governs the deductibility of SR&ED expenditures in computing a taxpayer's income from a business for a taxation year. Under ordinary income tax accounting principles, expenditures that generate enduring new knowledge, proprietary technology, and other intangible assets of a capital nature expected to yield economic benefits over multiple fiscal periods would be capitalized rather than deducted currently. Section 37 overrides this capital prohibition by allowing eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada to be deducted in full in the taxation year they are incurred, or alternatively accumulated in an indefinite "pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures" that can be carried forward perpetually to reduce taxable business income in any subsequent taxation year.

Following the 2024–2026 legislative reforms, subsection 37(1) operates through two primary paragraphs for domestic R&D outlays. Paragraph 37(1)(a) authorizes the deduction of expenditures of a current nature made by the taxpayer on SR&ED carried on in Canada, whether directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer or executed via eligible third-party payments to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, non-profit SR&ED corporations resident in Canada, or granting councils related to a business class of the taxpayer. Paragraph 37(1)(b), enacted by the 2025/2026 legislative amendments and effective for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, restores the eligibility of capital expenditures for immediate deduction against income under the SR&ED program. Specifically, paragraph 37(1)(b) captures expenditures of a capital nature made to acquire new or used depreciable property (excluding land and buildings) that the claimant intended to use all or substantially all (90% or more) of the operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada.

Additional provisions within section 37 safeguard the integrity of the deductible expenditure pool during corporate restructurings and third-party contracting. Subsection 37(6.1) governs the treatment of the unapplied section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool when a corporation undergoes a "loss restriction event" (such as an acquisition of control), streaming the carryforward pool so that it may only be deducted against future income from the same or a similar business. Furthermore, former subsection 37(14) (repealed by S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 5) established a statutory "look-through rule" for expenditures incurred by a taxpayer in respect of SR&ED performed on its behalf or by third-party entities, ensuring that ineligible capital outlays incurred prior to the December 16, 2024 restoration date were stripped out and only qualifying current expenditures were recognized.
Investment Tax Credit Architecture and Refundability: Sections 127 and 127.1

While section 37 governs the computation of net business income, section 127 of the ITA permits a taxpayer to claim Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) directly against Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, and section 127.1 authorizes the cash refundability of unused ITCs for eligible claimants. The interplay of these core statutory provisions is detailed in the legislative matrix below.

body.text: Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Caps, Phase-Outs, and the 2024–2026 Reforms

The financial quantum and cash refundability of a federal SR&ED claim depend upon four intersecting variables: the legal classification of the claimant, the commencement date of the taxation year relative to the December 16, 2024 legislative transition date, the character of the underlying expenditure (current versus capital), and the claimant's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada or prior three-year average consolidated revenue.
Basic vs. Enhanced Investment Tax Credit Rates

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the basic SR&ED ITC rate is 15% on qualified SR&ED expenditures. This 15% basic rate applies universally to corporations that do not qualify for the enhanced rate (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries, large public corporations exceeding revenue thresholds, and private corporations exceeding taxable capital limits), as well as to qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) in excess of their annual expenditure limit. The 15% basic rate also applies to unincorporated businesses, sole proprietorships (individuals), beneficiaries of trusts, and individual partners of a partnership.

Under subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, qualifying CCPCs—and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, qualifying ECPCs—earn an additional 20% ITC on top of the 15% basic rate, yielding a combined enhanced SR&ED ITC rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit.
Evolution of the Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

The annual "expenditure limit" establishes the maximum dollar volume of qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the 35% enhanced ITC in a full 365-day taxation year, subject to proration for short taxation years, multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year, and mandatory allocation among associated CCPCs or consolidated ECPC groups. A chronological audit of the Income Tax Act demonstrates how the expenditure limit has evolved across three distinct legislative eras.

In the first legislative era—spanning from February 26, 2008 (when the CCPC expenditure limit was increased from $2 million to $3 million) through March 19, 2019—a CCPC's $3 million expenditure limit was subject to a dual-factor phase-out based on both prior-year taxable income and prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. Specifically, the $3 million expenditure limit was reduced whenever the CCPC's (and associated group's) previous-year taxable income exceeded $500,000 (eliminated entirely at $800,000) or its previous-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeded $10 million (eliminated entirely at $50 million). During that period, whether a CCPC met the definition of a "qualifying corporation" eligible for 40% refundability on its 15% ITCs earned above the expenditure limit also hinged on whether its prior-year taxable income remained within its "qualifying income limit," defined in the ITA for 2010 and later taxation years by the formula:
Qualifying income limit = $500,000 × [($40 million − A) ÷ $40 million]

where A equalled nil if the prior-year taxable capital amount was less than or equal to $10 million, or the lesser of $40 million and the amount by which taxable capital exceeded $10 million in any other case.

In the second legislative era, initiated by Budget 2019 for taxation years ending after March 19, 2019, and continuing for all taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, Parliament repealed the use of previous-year taxable income as a factor in determining a CCPC's annual expenditure limit. Throughout this period, the maximum expenditure limit remained $3 million (exclusively for CCPCs), phasing out strictly on a straight-line basis when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated group reached $10 million and becoming nil starting at $50 million.

In the third and current legislative era, applicable to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (pursuant to the December 2024 reform announcement and the legislation granted Royal Assent on March 26, 2026), the maximum annual expenditure limit is doubled to $6 million. While interim August 2025 legislative explanatory notes issued by the Department of Finance initially modelled an expenditure limit up to $4.5 million under draft subsection 127(10.6), the final enacted framework administered by the CRA across its official May 2026 tax forms and SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy establishes the $6 million maximum annual expenditure limit for both CCPCs and ECPCs.

Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6 million expenditure limit is phased out over a substantially expanded $15 million to $75 million corridor using two distinct statutory methodologies depending on corporate status or election. Under subsection 127(10.2), for a CCPC using the standard Taxable Capital Method, the $6 million expenditure limit begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and its associated corporations) for the previous taxation year reaches $15 million and becomes nil starting at $75 million. Expressed mathematically for a 365-day taxation year, the CCPC expenditure limit under the post-December 15, 2024 rules is:

Expenditure limit = $6 million × [($60 million − A) ÷ $60 million], where A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (of the CCPC and its associated corporations) is $15 million or less, or otherwise the lesser of $60 million and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15 million.

Conversely, for an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) whose taxation year begins after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(10.6) determines the expenditure limit using an Average Revenue Method. The $6 million expenditure limit for an ECPC is reduced when the corporation's (or consolidated group's) average revenue over the previous three fiscal years exceeds $15 million, phasing out linearly until it becomes nil starting at $75 million. Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC or a group of associated CCPCs may formally elect, under prescribed conditions, to calculate its expenditure limit in the same way as an ECPC using the three-year average revenue test. Where a CCPC group makes this election for a taxation year, the expenditure limit based on taxable capital employed in Canada under subsection 127(10.2) ceases to apply to the group for that year. This statutory election eliminates a severe penalty that previously affected capital-intensive pre-revenue or early-stage CCPCs—such as biotechnology, semiconductor, or clean-tech enterprises—whose balance sheets held more than $15 million in paid-up capital stock or debt financing (which inflated their taxable capital employed in Canada) despite generating minimal commercial revenue.
Eligibility Requirements for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Extending the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to public corporations remedies a historical distortion in Canadian corporate finance, whereby a domestic technology company immediately forfeited its 35% refundable SR&ED rate upon executing an initial public offering (IPO) on a Canadian stock exchange. Under the post-December 15, 2024 statutory regime, a corporation qualifies as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) if it is resident in Canada, is a public corporation (or falls within prescribed public corporate rules rather than being a CCPC), and satisfies a strict non-resident control test. Specifically, the CRA and the ITA require that even if all the shares of the corporation owned by non-residents were instead owned by one particular hypothetical person, the ECPC would still not be controlled by that particular person. Where an ECPC belongs to a consolidated group of ECPCs, the expenditure limit must be calculated using the consolidated group's average revenue over the previous three fiscal years and shared among the group members included in the consolidated financial statements in accordance with subsection 127(10.61).
Comprehensive Summary of Federal SR&ED ITC Rates and Refundability

Under section 127.1 of the ITA, the cash refundability of earned SR&ED ITCs differs substantially between expenditures of a current nature and restored expenditures of a capital nature. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, both qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 100% refund on the 35% enhanced ITC attributable to current expenditures up to their expenditure limit, whereas the 35% enhanced ITC earned on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit is 40% refundable. Moreover, subsection 127.1(2.01) specifically preserves the 100% refundability of the 35% ITC on current expenditures (and 40% on capital expenditures) up to the reduced expenditure limit for a CCPC that is neither a "qualifying corporation" nor an "excluded corporation" (i.e., a CCPC operating within the phase-out corridor). On expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit, a qualifying CCPC earns the 15% basic ITC with 40% refundability, whereas phase-out CCPCs, ECPCs, and other corporations earn a non-refundable 15% ITC above the limit. Individuals, sole proprietors, certain trusts, and individual partners of a partnership earn the 15% basic ITC and obtain a 40% cash refund after applying the credit against any income tax owing.

body.text: Carryforward, Carryback, and Taxation of Assistance and ITCs

Where a claimant earns non-refundable SR&ED ITCs (or elects not to utilize a credit in the current year), unused federal SR&ED ITCs do not expire at year-end; under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, they may be carried back up to 3 taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years to be applied against federal Part I income tax payable in those years.

To prevent double subsidization of the same underlying expenditure, the Income Tax Act enforces rigorous accounting adjustments between government assistance, federal ITCs, and the section 37 income deduction pool. In the taxation year in which SR&ED expenditures are incurred, all provincial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit, the Québec CRIC, the British Columbia SR&ED tax credit, or the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant), direct federal or provincial grants, and non-government assistance that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive must be deducted from both the section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool (reported on Lines 429, 431, and 432 of Form T661) and the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool for federal ITC purposes (reported on Line 513 of Form T661). If the taxpayer subsequently repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED pools, that repayment is added back to the section 37 deductible pool (on Line 445 of Schedule B / Form T661) and to qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (on Line 560 of Form T661) in the year of repayment.

Furthermore, any federal SR&ED ITCs applied against Part I tax payable and/or refunded in cash in a taxation year reduce the claimant's section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year, as reported on Line 435 of Form T661. Where a claimant deducts its entire section 37 pool in the current year, the subsequent year's pool reduction on Line 435 will create a negative balance in the section 37 pool that must be included in taxable business income for that following year.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies

To qualify for inclusion on Form T661, an outlay must be incurred in respect of eligible SR&ED work carried on in Canada and satisfy the statutory parameters governing salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, subcontractor and third-party payments, overhead, or restored capital property and shared-use equipment.
Salaries and Wages: Non-Specified vs. Specified Employees and Foreign Rules

Labour expenditures constitute the primary cost driver for most Canadian SR&ED claimants. Under section 37 and subsection 127(9), only the portion of an employee's salary or wages that directly relates to the time the employee was actively engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED is eligible. The ITA strictly differentiates between regular arm's-length employees ("employees other than specified employees") and "specified employees".

For employees other than specified employees—comprising arm's-length engineers, scientists, software developers, technicians, and first-line technical supervisors who own less than 10% of the shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation—100% of their SR&ED-apportioned salaries, wages, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are included in the section 37 current expenditure pool. However, if the claimant elects to use the Proxy Method to calculate notional overhead, all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits that were included on Line 810 of Part 5 of Form T661 must be subtracted on Line 812 to arrive at the eligible salary base on Line 814.

A specified employee, by contrast, is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the claimant or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly, at least 10% of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation. For specified employees (tracked individually by name on Line 850 of Form T661), all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are completely disallowed for SR&ED purposes, and total eligible SR&ED salary or wages are capped at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated for the number of days employed in the year. Additionally, when computing the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base in Part 5 of Form T661, a specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits on Line 852) is subject to an overarching proxy inclusion ceiling equal to the lesser of 75% of that total salary on Line 852 and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated by days employed.

While SR&ED expenditures must generally be incurred for work carried out within Canada, the ITA provides a limited statutory exception for permissible foreign salaries. Claimants must indicate on Line 265 of Part 2 of Form T661 whether they are claiming salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada for a project. Such outside-Canada salary or wages paid to Canadian-resident employees are allowable only if the work is directly undertaken by the claimant (not subcontracted), forms an integral component of an SR&ED project carried on in Canada, and does not exceed 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages incurred for work performed inside Canada during the taxation year.
Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Expenditures on tangible physical materials qualify for SR&ED treatment when the materials are either consumed (destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during experimental trials) or transformed (integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or trial production run) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. The CRA strictly enforces the rule against excess production, defined as any production beyond what is technically required for the experimental validation of the SR&ED hypothesis; all costs associated with excess production are excluded. Moreover, where materials transformed during an SR&ED project result in production output (output from an experimental process or prototype) that is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, clawback and recapture rules require the claimant to reduce its SR&ED pool by the lesser of the original cost of the materials and the proceeds of disposition or fair market value of the commercial output.
Subcontractors, Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

Canadian tax law establishes distinct inclusion rules for arm's-length SR&ED subcontractors, non-arm's-length performers, and third-party institutional research payments. When a claimant engages an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor to perform SR&ED work in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is deductible in the section 37 expenditure pool, but only 80% of the eligible contract payment qualifies for earning the federal SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(9). Following the restoration of capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, capital expenditures for depreciable property or equipment lease costs incurred by a contractor before December 16, 2024, remain strictly disqualified under the look-through rule of former subsection 37(14), whereas amounts related to depreciable property acquired by the performer after December 15, 2024, are separately tracked and reported on Lines 535 and 540 of Form T661.

Where SR&ED work is contracted between persons not dealing at arm's length (such as parent and subsidiary corporations), the contract payment itself does not directly earn an ITC for the payer; instead, the parties must execute Form T1146, Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length (with the performer reporting the agreed transferred amount on Line 540 of Form T661), and may allocate related government assistance using Form T1145, Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length.

Distinct from bilateral service contracts, third-party payments are reported on Line 370 of Form T661 and itemized on a separate Schedule A (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment. Eligible third-party recipients include an approved university, college, research institute, or other similar institution (Line 714), a non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada (Line 712), or a granting council (Line 716), where the payment funds basic research (Line 734), applied research, or experimental development (Line 731) in Canada related to a business of the claimant and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. In addition, transactions by agricultural organizations through producer levies are governed by section 8.0 of the CRA Third-Party Payments Policy, whereby SR&ED transactions by agricultural organizations constitute transactions made by the producers themselves.
Overhead and Other Expenditures: Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (PPA)

To account for indirect and overhead costs associated with conducting R&D, a claimant must make an annual election on Form T661 between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method. The structural differences between these two computational methodologies are summarized in the comparison table below.

body.text: Restored Capital Expenditures (Line 390) and Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures for depreciable property and equipment lease costs were completely excluded from the federal SR&ED tax incentive program. Pursuant to the 2024–2026 legislative reforms, expenditures for depreciable property or for the right to use property acquired after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024) once again qualify for SR&ED tax incentives across two primary capital mechanisms: All or Substantially All (ASA) SR&ED capital expenditures on Line 390, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504. Any expenditures for depreciable property or lease costs incurred before December 16, 2024, remain strictly ineligible.

Under the first mechanism, an SR&ED capital expenditure (Line 390 of Form T661) is an expenditure made by a claimant to acquire new or used depreciable property (for which the claimant would otherwise be allowed to claim capital cost allowance, and which became available for use after December 15, 2024) that the claimant intended to use in one of two ways: either to use all or substantially all (ASA)—defined as 90% or more—of the operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada. Land is a non-depreciable asset and buildings are generally excluded from eligibility. Allowable capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 are combined with allowable current expenditures from Line 380 to form total allowable SR&ED expenditures on Line 400 (entering the section 37 deductible expenditure pool) and also earn SR&ED ITCs (with the 35% enhanced ITC on capital expenditures being 40% refundable for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs). Because 100% of the capital cost is claimed via Line 390, the CRA mandates that capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8, Capital Cost Allowance (CCA). Furthermore, claimants claiming capital expenditures on Line 390 must report on Lines 262 and 263 of Part 2 of Form T661 the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties acquired after December 15, 2024, used in each project.

Under the second mechanism, depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA test may still qualify for SR&ED ITCs as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 if it is used primarily—defined for SR&ED purposes as more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time—for SR&ED in Canada. Generally, "operating time" means the time the equipment usually runs or functions; if a claimant's taxation year began before December 16, 2024, and straddled the effective date, the claimant must calculate SR&ED use as a percentage of total operating time for the period after December 15, 2024. If the equipment meets the requirements of both first-term and second-term SUE, the claimant claims on Line 504: 25% of the capital cost of the equipment that was used primarily in SR&ED in the first period (first-term SUE), and the other 25% of the capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE). The SR&ED ITC calculation for SUE is identical under both the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method. However, unlike ASA capital expenditures on Line 390, the capital cost of SUE is not part of the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the claimant must depreciate the capital cost of SUE under the regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rates and rules on Schedule T2SCH8. Claimants must also list on Form T661 the names of the 20 most expensive SUE properties acquired after December 15, 2024.

Finally, if depreciable property (whether ASA or SUE) for which an SR&ED ITC was claimed is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, ITC Recapture rules apply. The claimant (or members of a partnership) must calculate the recapture amount using Schedule T2SCH31, Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, or Form T2038(IND), Investment Tax Credit (Individuals), and add the recaptured amount directly to Part I Tax Payable for that year.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nearly every Canadian province and the Yukon Territory supplement the federal SR&ED program with regional R&D tax credits. With the exception of Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency through schedules attached to the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return or T1 individual return. Because every provincial or territorial credit constitutes "provincial government assistance," the dollar amount of any provincial credit earned (unless formally renounced where permitted by provincial law) reduces the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base on Line 513 (and Line 429) of federal Form T661.
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario delivers corporate R&D tax relief through three distinct statutory credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA for non-exempt corporations that maintain a permanent establishment in Ontario, carry on eligible SR&ED in Ontario, are eligible to claim a federal ITC under section 127 of the federal ITA, and have filed federal Form T661.

The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566 (T2SCH566) alongside mandatory prescribed federal Schedule T2SCH31, provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016 (reduced from 10% for taxation years ending before June 1, 2016) on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3 million, yielding a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000. Associated corporations must share the $3 million expenditure limit, and the limit is prorated for short taxation years based on the number of days in the taxation year relative to 365. Unlike the federal SR&ED regime (which repealed its taxable income phase-out in 2019 and expanded its capital thresholds in 2024), the OITC retains a dual phase-out mechanism: the $3 million expenditure limit is gradually reduced if the prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25 million and $50 million. Critically, in parallel with the federal December 2024 reforms, Ontario updated the OITC so that qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (whereas capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013, and before December 16, 2024, were excluded, and pre-2014 capital expenditures were included at 40%).

The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508 (T2SCH508) alongside mandatory prescribed federal Schedule T2SCH31, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016 (reduced from 4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) with no expenditure cap, available to all corporations to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. Any unused portion of the ORDTC may be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years. To prevent intra-provincial double-dipping, the OITC is treated as government assistance that directly reduces the eligible expenditure base for the ORDTC. Under certain conditions, corporations dealing at non-arm's length may file an agreement to transfer eligible ORDTC expenditures. In alignment with federal reforms, the ORDTC includes 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (as well as 100% of pre-2014 capital expenditures, while excluding capital outlays between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024). If property included in a previous ORDTC claim is subsequently disposed of or converted to commercial use, Ontario recapture rules apply using a 23.56% rate to calculate recapture. (Additionally, specified corporations subject to Ontario transitional tax debits or credits utilize Schedules T2SCH506 and T2SCH507).

The Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), governed by section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and claimed on Schedule 568 (T2SCH568) and Schedule 569 (T2SCH569) (Contract Information), provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures (up to a $20 million annual cap) incurred under an eligible research contract with an approved Ontario research institute. Unlike the OITC and ORDTC, Ontario law does not require prescribed federal Schedule T2SCH31 to be filed to claim the OBRITC.
Québec: The 2025–2026 Consolidation into the CRIC Regime

Québec operates an autonomous corporate income tax regime administered by Revenu Québec, with sectoral and institutional certifications issued by the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy (ministre de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie) under the Act respecting the sectoral parameters of certain fiscal measures.

In the Québec Budget 2025–2026 (tabled March 25, 2025), the Québec government enacted a sweeping structural consolidation of its R&D tax incentives for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Specifically, Québec abolished six legacy R&D and design tax credits: (1) the Tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D); (2) the Tax credit for university research and for research carried on by a public research centre or a research consortium; (3) the Tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research; (4) the Tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium (though an eligible fee balance at the end of a tax year or fiscal period ending after March 25, 2025, can still give rise to the consortium credit under transitional rules for a tax year ending on or before December 31, 2029); (5) the Tax credit for technological adaptation services; and (6) the industrial design component of the Tax credit for an in-house design activity (leaving only the fashion design component unchanged).

Replacing these six abolished programs is the unified, 100% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC). Whereas Québec's legacy R&D salary tax credit restricted its enhanced 30% rate to SMEs with less than $50 million in assets (phasing down to 14% at $75 million in assets), the CRIC's two-tier rate structure depends solely on the level of qualified spending rather than company asset size. Under the CRIC, all eligible Québec corporations (and corporate members of eligible partnerships) earn a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above the annual exclusion threshold (with the $1 million expenditure limit shared among an associated corporate group and prorated for short taxation years of less than 51 weeks), and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on all additional eligible expenditures exceeding that first $1,000,000.

The CRIC also significantly broadens the base of eligible Québec expenditures to encompass: 100% of salaries and wages for R&D and pre-commercialization staff in Québec; 50% of subcontractor expenses for work performed in Québec; 50% of contract payments or fees paid to eligible Québec universities, public research centres, or research consortia (for which the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues to issue recognition certificates); and 100% of capital expenditures on new depreciable property used in R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec (subject to limitations where property is used as part of a large investment project benefitting from a tax holiday).

Notably left unchanged under the CRIC is Québec's mandatory exclusion threshold: to claim the CRIC, a corporation's qualified expenditures must exceed an annual threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec basic personal amounts for R&D employees ($18,571 per full-time equivalent R&D employee in 2025). For example, if a corporation employs one full-time R&D employee in 2025, its exclusion threshold is $50,000 (since 1 × $18,571 = $18,571 is less than $50,000), whereas if it employs five full-time R&D employees, its exclusion threshold is $92,855 (5 × $18,571). For a Québec startup incurring $2,000,000 in qualified expenditures with a $50,000 exclusion threshold (eligible base of $1,950,000), generating a refundable CRIC of $300,000 (30% × $1,000,000) plus $190,000 (20% × $950,000), for a total Québec credit of $490,000—which then reduces the federal SR&ED expenditure base as provincial assistance. (In a parallel technology measure effective for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, Québec also reformed its multimedia/IT credits by adding data processing and hosting activities to promote the eligibility of artificial intelligence businesses while removing maintenance or evolution activities).
British Columbia: Permanent SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666)

Governed by sections 97 to 103 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia), the British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit is now a permanent provincial incentive administered by the CRA for corporations with a permanent establishment in British Columbia. Practitioners must distinguish Form T666, British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit (which is the prescribed form for claiming the BC SR&ED credit, alongside Schedule 5, Tax Calculation Supplementary – Corporations) from Schedule 421 (T2SCH421), which is the British Columbia Mining Exploration Tax Credit under section 25.1 of the BC ITA. The BC SR&ED credit provides a 10% refundable credit for qualifying CCPCs up to their $3 million expenditure limit and a 10% non-refundable credit for other corporations or CCPCs on expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit (with a 3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward, and the statutory ability to renounce non-refundable credits only).
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — AT1 Schedule 29)

Effective for eligible expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020, Alberta provides the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) under Division 7 of Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act. Overseen by the Ministry of Technology and Innovation and administered independently by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) (located at 9811 109 Street NW, Edmonton, AB T5K 2L5) pursuant to Information Circular IEG-1R5 and the Guide to Claiming the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant, the IEG is a fully refundable tax credit claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and accompanied by Form AT4970, Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta, with the net credit reported on Line 129 of the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1).

The IEG delivers a two-tier incremental refundable benefit on up to a $4 million annual maximum expenditure limit (prorated for short taxation years and allocated among associated corporations via page 3 of Form AT29). Under Part I of Form AT29 (Line 110), a qualified corporation earns an 8% base payment on the lesser of its eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures (matching federal Line 559/557 of Form T661 for work carried out in Alberta) and its allocated expenditure limit. Under Part II of Form AT29 (Line 125), the corporation earns an additional 12% payment—bringing the total support rate to an enhanced 20% payment—on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's base level of spending. A firm's base level of spending is calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years; if a corporation had no eligible Alberta expenditures in the preceding two years, its base amount is nil ($0), allowing its entire current-year Alberta spending up to the limit to earn the combined 20% rate. The $4 million expenditure limit phases out incrementally for firms with between $10 million and $50 million in prior-year taxable capital, and firms with $50 million or more in taxable capital are ineligible.

Because the IEG constitutes provincial government assistance that reduces federal qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 513 of federal Form T661, TRA mandates a two-step calculation on Form AT29 to prevent a circular calculation. In Step 1, the claimant calculates the preliminary IEG (Line 130 of Form AT29) based on federal qualified/current expenditures before deducting the IEG on Line 513 of federal Form T661. In Step 2, the claimant includes that Line 130 preliminary IEG amount on Line 513 of federal Form T661 as provincial government assistance, enters the recalculated federal amount from Line 559 of Form T661 onto Line 003 of Form AT29, and adds back the Step 1 IEG on Line 011 of Form AT29 to compute the final net IEG on Line 134 (transferred to Line 129 of the AT1 return). If an IEG claim is rejected solely because Schedule 29 was filed after the statutory 15-month filing deadline, TRA sends a rejection letter rather than an assessment, though TRA accepts formal notices of objection to review the timing of the filing.

body.text: Administrative Governance, Filing Mechanics, Form T661 Structure, and Statutory Deadlines

The Canada Revenue Agency administers the SR&ED program through specialized regional Tax Services Offices—such as the Fraser Valley and Interior Tax Services Office for Saskatchewan and western claimants—governed by the CRA SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy and T4088 – Guide to Form T661 – Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim. Following Royal Assent of the SR&ED legislative enhancements on March 26, 2026, the CRA released updated prescribed forms in May 2026: Form T661 (published May 15, 2026), Form T1145 (May 15, 2026), Form T1146 (May 15, 2026), T2 Schedule 31 (T2SCH31) (May 22, 2026), and T2 Schedule 49 (T2SCH49), Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit (May 29, 2026).
Line-by-Line Architecture of Prescribed Form T661 (May 2026 Revision)

To access both the section 37 expenditure pool deduction and the section 127 ITC, a claimant must file Form T661 containing all prescribed information, accompanied by Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations (completing the corporation's name, business number, tax year-end, and parts 2, 3, 8 to 17, 29, and 30) or Form T2038(IND) for individuals and trusts (completing parts A to F). Because Form T661 includes electronic fields for all prescribed information, claimants filing electronically via certified tax preparation software must not submit duplicate paper copies.

Form T661 is organized into 10 statutorily prescribed parts. Part 1 (General Information) captures claimant identification and corporate group status. Part 2 (Project Information: Sections A to C) captures technical narratives, classification codes, authorship, capital asset lists, and contemporaneous documentation checklists through a series of prescribed fields. While a separate Part 2 is required for each project claimed, claimants with more than 20 projects may choose to submit Part 2 with their return for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided they include the costs of every project in Part 6 and maintain completed Part 2 forms for all remaining projects at their place of business ready for submission upon CRA demand (failure to provide them upon request results in complete disallowance of the project's expenditures).

Within Part 2 of the May 2026 revision of Form T661, Line 207 requires the five-digit Field of Research code (RDF#####) from Statistics Canada's Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0 (beginning on page 18 of the CRDC manual) that best describes the primary field of science or technology. If the claimant obtained pre-claim project approval through the CRA's pre-claim approval process, they tick the box on Line 212 and enter the pre-claim approval case number on Line 214. In Section B of Part 2 (which since December 2014 consolidated all project narratives onto Lines 242 to 246, replacing legacy lines 248 to 252), the claimant must set out: the scientific or technological uncertainties attempted to be overcome (Line 242), the systematic experimental or analytical work performed in the taxation year to overcome those uncertainties (Line 244), and the resulting scientific or technological advancements achieved or attempted (Line 246). Lines 253 to 259 require mandatory disclosure of who prepared the technical descriptions in Section B: ticking Line 253 and naming the individual on Line 254 if prepared by a directly involved employee who performed or directly supervised the SR&ED work described at Line 244; ticking Line 255 and naming the employee on Line 256 if prepared by a non-directly involved employee; or ticking Line 257 and providing the consultant's name and firm on Lines 258 and 259 if prepared by an external consultant. Lines 260 and 261 list the names, position titles (using "contractor" if applicable), and relevant technical qualifications/experience of up to three key individuals directly involved in the project. Newly added Lines 262 and 263 require the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024, used in each project and claimed on Line 390, while Line 265 indicates whether outside-Canada salary or wages are claimed.

Part 3 (Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures: Sections A to C) computes allowable current SR&ED expenditures (Line 380, incorporating overhead on Line 360 if using the Traditional Method and third-party payments on Line 370), restored SR&ED capital expenditures (Line 390), and total allowable SR&ED expenditures (Line 400). Part 3 then adjusts the section 37 deductible expenditure pool by subtracting provincial government assistance (Line 429), other government assistance (Line 431), non-government assistance (Line 432), prior-year SR&ED ITCs applied and/or refunded (Line 435), and proceeds from the sale of SR&ED capital assets (Line 440), while adding back repayments of assistance (Line 445) and pool transfers from amalgamations or wind-ups (Line 452) before arriving at the current-year SR&ED deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1. Part 4 (Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes) adds the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), deducts provincial and other assistance (Line 513) and non-qualifying capital contract amounts (Lines 535 and 540), and determines qualified SR&ED expenditures (Line 559) and total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (Line 570) after repayments made in the year (Line 560).

Part 5 (Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount) computes the 55% notional overhead base across regular employees (Lines 810–814) and specified employees (Lines 850–852). Part 6 (Project Costs) requires expenditures to be recorded and allocated on a project-by-project basis for every project claimed in the year. Part 7 (Additional Information) captures statistical data on sources of funds and the distribution of basic research, applied research, and experimental development, while Part 8 (Claim Checklist) provides a compliance verification list. Finally, Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) mandates complete disclosure for every claim preparer that has accepted consideration to prepare or assist in the preparation of the SR&ED claim, followed by Part 10 (Certification) signed by an authorized officer. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA, if prescribed information in Part 9 regarding the claim preparer(s) and billing arrangement(s) is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable, although an omission in Part 9 does not itself disallow the underlying SR&ED claim.
Statutory Reporting Deadlines by Taxpayer Type

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the ITA and section 5.2 of the CRA SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, the statutory reporting deadline to file Form T661 and to include the ITC earned on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is strictly 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. If a claimant fails to file the prescribed information by this statutory reporting deadline, the SR&ED claim is statutorily barred and rejected. When an SR&ED reporting deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or public holiday recognized by the CRA, the claim is considered filed on time if the CRA receives it or if it is postmarked on or before the next business day.

body.text: Judicial Precedents, Audit Standards, and Contemporaneous Documentation

When the CRA reviews an SR&ED claim, it evaluates both whether the work satisfies the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA and whether the claimed expenditures are supported by contemporaneous documentary and financial evidence. Furthermore, taxpayers enjoy statutory procedural protections during investigations; as confirmed in Gordon et al v. The King, the CRA's investigation into SR&ED tax credits must respect statutory boundaries regarding its audit and investigative powers, while strict statutory limitation periods apply to filing notices of objection under section 166.2 of the ITA, which common-law duties of procedural fairness cannot override (Odebala-Fregene, 2015 DTC 1087).
The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies

The bedrock of Canadian SR&ED substantive law is the seminal 1998 Tax Court of Canada judgment by Judge Donald Bowman (later Chief Justice Bowman) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (T.C.C.), which was subsequently adopted and articulated as five binding questions by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2000 D.T.C. (T.C.C.) / 2002 D.T.C. 6740 (F.C.A.).

In Northwest Hydraulic, Judge Bowman examined the legislative intent of Parliament in enacting the SR&ED tax incentives—citing Conoltex Inc. v. R., (1997), 97 D.T.C. 724 (T.C.C.) for the proposition that the provisions are intended to encourage scientific research in Canada and should be interpreted with an approach that gives effect to that incentive purpose—while translating the concepts of Information Circular IC 86-4 into five cumulative judicial criteria. As summarized by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393) and consistently applied by the Tax Court of Canada in cases such as National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2019 TCC 166 (at paragraph 11) and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC), a taxpayer bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that all five questions are answered in the affirmative:

First, was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Being faced with an uncertain commercial path toward an objective is not, by itself, sufficient to qualify a project as SR&ED; the taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities that the underlying technical uncertainty could not be resolved through routine engineering, standard procedures, or normal analyses carried out by competent professionals using current technology and techniques.

Second, did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? The claimant must demonstrate that it moved beyond ad-hoc guesswork by articulating specific scientific or technological hypotheses directed at solving the identified uncertainty.

Third, did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? The investigation must follow a systematic protocol of observation, hypothesis formulation, rigorous experimental testing or analysis, and iterative hypothesis modification based on the observed test results.

Fourth, did the process result in a technological advancement? The work must seek to advance technological knowledge or capability beyond standard practice, rather than merely assembling known components via established methodologies.

Fifth, was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed? As Judge Bowman famously emphasized in Northwest Hydraulic—a principle highlighted by the Office of the Taxpayers' Ombudsperson in its review of service fairness within the SR&ED program—maintaining contemporaneous documentation recorded as the experimental work progresses is essential to corroborate that systematic scientific investigation actually occurred.
Evolution of Subsequent Jurisprudence Across Industrial Sectors

Subsequent rulings of the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal illustrate how the five-question framework operates across software development, manufacturing, custom engineering, and food/beverage science, as detailed in the jurisprudential matrix below.

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (T.C.C.)
Established the foundational 5-criteria test for SR&ED under s. 248(1) based on IC 86-4; cited Conoltex Inc. v. R. (97 D.T.C. 724) on parliamentary intent to encourage scientific research in Canada.
Defines the boundary between "routine engineering" and genuine "technological uncertainty" and establishes the necessity of contemporaneous documentation.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (F.C.A.)
Formally adopted Judge Bowman's 5 criteria into five binding appellate questions for determining whether development expenses constitute SR&ED.
Elevates the 5-question framework to binding Federal Court of Appeal precedent across all Canadian jurisdictions.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261; aff'd 2011 FCA 355
Affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal; disallowed claims where shop-floor modifications lacked systematic hypothesis formulation and adherence to the scientific method.
Confirms that trial-and-error manufacturing adjustments without structured experimental protocols fail Questions 2, 3, and 5.
Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65, 2015 D.T.C. 1089

Taxpayer claimed SR&ED for 2012 expenses incurred in developing a computer software program capable of inspecting and verifying websites. Appeal dismissed: activities constituted nothing more than normal analyses carried out by competent programmers using current technology and techniques (though deductible as ordinary business expenses).

Establishes a rigorous threshold for software SR&ED: complex programming using existing tools and techniques does not satisfy s. 248(1) or C.W. Agencies unless genuine technological uncertainty is proven.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6
Examined custom mechanical rigging projects under the 5-question test; distinguished custom engineering design from resolving underlying technological uncertainty.
Demonstrates that bespoke engineering and first-of-a-kind commercial builds require proof that standard engineering procedures could not achieve the objective.
National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2019 TCC 166
At paragraph 11, Justice Russell reaffirmed the five questions from Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies as the governing legal standard.
Reinforces the strict evidentiary burden on claimants to substantiate each of the five questions objectively.
Tax Court of Canada ruled that the experimental development of a commercial food recipe qualifies for SR&ED credits where the five C.W. Agencies questions are met.
Confirms that food science and agricultural processing qualify for SR&ED when resolving genuine biochemical, texture, or preservation uncertainties systematically.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC)

Allowed taxpayer's appeal for the 2020 taxation year (ended July 31, 2020) regarding development of a non-refrigerated beverage ("Chrisoda"). Although Form T661 did not explicitly state the objective was a non-refrigerated product, credible testimony and contemporaneous documents recording hypotheses, testing, and test results satisfied all 5 questions on a balance of probabilities.

Illustrates that while Form T661 narratives should be carefully drafted, the Tax Court prioritizes contemporaneous experimental records of hypotheses, testing, and results when adjudicating substantive SR&ED eligibility.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions and Audit Risk Mitigation Recommendations

A holistic synthesis of Canada's federal and provincial R&D tax architecture following the 2024–2026 legislative reforms demonstrates a decisive policy realignment toward capital-intensive domestic R&D, scaling mid-market enterprises, and Canadian-controlled public corporations. To maximize statutory entitlement while insulating claims against Canada Revenue Agency, Revenu Québec, and Alberta TRA audit adjustments, corporate taxpayers and their advisors should execute a disciplined, five-pillar compliance strategy.

First, enterprises acquiring laboratory, prototyping, or industrial equipment on or after December 16, 2024, must immediately implement machine-hour telemetry and operating-time logs to substantiate the distinction between All or Substantially All (ASA) capital property (90% or more SR&ED operating time or value consumption, claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 and excluded from Schedule T2SCH8 CCA) and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (more than 50% but less than 90% SR&ED operating time, claimed at 25% in the first term and 25% in the second term on Line 504 while depreciated under regular Schedule T2SCH8 CCA rules). Claimants must also ensure that the 10 most expensive ASA capital properties per project are itemized on Lines 262 and 263 of Form T661 and the 20 most expensive SUE properties are properly scheduled.

Second, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, capital-intensive CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15 million should model the newly enacted statutory election to compute their $6 million expenditure limit under the ECPC three-year average revenue method (subsection 127(10.6)) rather than the taxable capital method (subsection 127(10.2)). Where a CCPC holds substantial equity or debt financing on its balance sheet to fund multi-year R&D but generates less than $15 million in three-year average revenue, electing into the ECPC calculation preserves the full $6 million expenditure limit and up to $2.1 million in annual 35% enhanced federal ITCs.

Third, multi-provincial claimants must adapt their accounting systems to regional structural reforms enacted in 2025 and 2026. In Ontario, claimants should capture post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures on both Schedule 566 (OITC) and Schedule 508 (ORDTC). In Québec, corporations must transition from the six abolished legacy credits to the unified CRIC regime for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, factoring in the $50,000 (or, if greater, the sum of R&D employees' basic personal amounts) exclusion threshold and capturing newly eligible R&D and pre-commercialization capital assets to earn the 30% credit on the first $1 million and 20% on excess spending.
